overview: Olaf IV of Norway was son of Margaret I whose short reign united Danish and Norwegian succession before his early death. The profile is anchored by concrete turning points: 1376 — Becomes king of Denmark; 1380 — Becomes king of Norway.
He died in 1387, and his reign belongs to the wider story of Scandinavian state formation, Christianization, dynastic conflict, and northern Europe’s ties to England, the Baltic, and the Empire.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Olaf IV of Norway was son of Margaret I whose short reign united Danish and Norwegian succession before his early death. The profile is anchored by concrete turning points: 1376 — Becomes king of Denmark; 1380 — Becomes king of Norway.
He died in 1387, and his reign belongs to the wider story of Scandinavian state formation, Christianization, dynastic conflict, and northern Europe’s ties to England, the Baltic, and the Empire.

contentSections.title: Birth and early life
paragraphs: Olaf IV of Norway was born c. 1370. His family background is usually placed in Bjälbo / Estridsen line, though early Scandinavian genealogy can be uncertain and politically shaped.
Olaf IV of Norway's early life belonged to the medieval Scandinavian world, where kinship, sea routes, church contacts, assemblies, and armed followings shaped the opportunities available to a ruler.

contentSections.title: Character and Personality
paragraphs: Olaf IV of Norway died at about seventeen, and almost nothing of a personal character can be recovered from so brief and so closely supervised a life. Born to Haakon VI and Margaret I, he was a child-king in whose name his mother governed, and the record concerns his dynastic significance — his claims to Norway, Denmark, and, through his father, to Sweden — rather than any individual temperament.

His sudden death in 1387 was the hinge on which Scandinavian history turned, since it freed Margaret to consolidate power directly and move toward the Kalmar Union. A strange afterlife followed: a pretender later appeared in the Baltic claiming to be the supposedly dead Olaf, an episode that says more about the uncertainty around his death than about the boy himself.

The honest assessment is that Olaf is a figure of dynastic potential cut short, not a recoverable personality. He is remembered for the consequences of his birth and early death rather than for anything he did or was said to be, his short life lived entirely within his mother's political design.

contentSections.title: As king of Denmark and Norway
paragraphs: Olaf became king of Denmark as a child and later king of Norway. Real power was exercised by Margaret I, but his position gave her the dynastic basis for wider rule.
As King of Denmark, King of Norway, Olaf IV of Norway had to turn dynastic claim into workable authority through alliances, military pressure, church support, and acceptance by regional elites.

contentSections.title: Death
paragraphs: Died suddenly at Falsterbo in 1387, creating a succession crisis that Margaret I navigated toward Scandinavian union.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: His short life mattered because it opened the path for Margaret’s rule and the Kalmar Union.
Later saga, saintly, or national traditions often amplified Olaf IV of Norway's reputation, so the article separates near-contemporary evidence from later memory where possible.

timeline.title: Becomes king of Norway
